title: What is it that “withholdeth”, and who is “he who now letteth” (2 Thessalonians 2:6–7)?
summary: 2 Thessalonians 2:6 says “now ye know what withholdeth that he might be revealed in his time”, and 2:7 says “only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way”. The passage does not name what withholds, who it is that restrains, or when and how he is taken out of the way.
text: KJV 2 Thessalonians 2:6: “now ye know what withholdeth that he might be revealed in his time”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) 2 Thessalonians 2:6: τὸ κατέχον οἴδατε [the restraining thing you know]. KJV 2 Thessalonians 2:7: “only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) 2 Thessalonians 2:7: μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται [only the one restraining now, until he comes out of the midst]. KJV 2 Thessalonians 2:5: “when I was yet with you, I told you these things”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/53/2/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/53/2/.
reasoning: The passage refers to what Paul had already told the readers (2:5) and so does not say what is meant. The restraint is first named as a thing (neuter, “what withholdeth”) and then as a person (masculine, “he who now letteth”); the text does not say whether these are one subject or two, what they hold back (the revealing of the man of lawlessness in 2:3, or the working of the mystery of iniquity in 2:7), or who removes the restrainer. Readings that name a government, a power of order, a person or a spiritual being are held as possibilities only; the text does not choose among them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to 2 Thessalonians 2:5–7. The record does not say which reading is right and does not claim that no other passage of the Bible says more. title: Which letter is “the epistle from Laodicea” (Colossians 4:16)?
summary: Colossians 4:16 tells the readers to see that “this epistle” is read in the church of the Laodiceans and that they “likewise read the epistle from Laodicea”. The verse does not say who wrote that letter, whether it was written by Paul to the Laodiceans or to someone else, or what became of it.
text: KJV Colossians 4:16: “cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) Colossians 4:16: ἀναγνωσθῇ, καὶ τὴν ἐκ [be read, and the one from (Laodicea)]. KJV Colossians 4:15: “Salute the brethren which are in Laodicea”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/51/4/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/51/4/.
reasoning: The Greek phrase is “the one from Laodicea”, with the word for letter understood from the earlier clause. The verse does not say whether this is a letter written to the Laodiceans (the sense of “to” is not in the words), a letter that reached Laodicea from another writer, or a letter that passed through the city on its way. It does not say whether it survives. Different readings are held as possibilities only; the text does not choose among them.

title: Who is “the mediator”, and what is the role of “angels” (Galatians 3:19–20)?
summary: Galatians 3:19 says the law “was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator”, and 3:20 adds “a mediator is not a mediator of one, but God is one”. The passage does not name the mediator, say which angels are meant or what they did, or say how the second sentence explains the first.
text: KJV Galatians 3:19: “it was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) Galatians 3:19: διαταγεὶς δι’ ἀγγέλων ἐν χειρὶ μεσίτου [ordered through angels in the hand of a mediator]. KJV Galatians 3:20: “a mediator is not a mediator of one, but God is one”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) Galatians 3:20: ὁ δὲ μεσίτης ἑνὸς οὐκ ἔστιν [but a mediator is not of one]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/48/3/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/48/3/.
reasoning: The verse does not say who the mediator is. It does not say what the angels did (delivered, ordered or attended the giving of the law), and 3:20 states a general principle about mediators without applying it. Different readings (a human mediator, a messenger of God, or another figure; angels as agents or as attendants) are held as possibilities only; the text does not choose among them.
